analysis.one_liner: Makes hospitals eat the cost when patients scheduled for surgery get surprise out-of-network bills.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its introduction, dying in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When you schedule a non-emergency procedure at a hospital that is in your insurance network, the hospital would have to ask you at scheduling whether you want in-network treatment only. If you say yes and the hospital still uses an out-of-network doctor anyway — say an anesthesiologist not covered by your plan — the hospital, not you or your insurer, would pay the extra cost. The rule is written as a condition of Medicare participation, so every hospital that takes Medicare patients would have to follow it.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and other insured patients who schedule non-emergency procedures at in-network hospitals. Today a patient can do everything right — pick an in-network hospital, confirm the hospital is covered — and still get a large bill from an out-of-network anesthesiologist or pathologist the patient never chose. Under this bill the patient could declare 'in-network only' at scheduling, and any out-of-network overage would be billed to the hospital instead. The patient's insurer would also stop absorbing those extra charges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients scheduling procedures at in-network hospitals

how_it_helps.text: At the time of scheduling, the hospital must give the patient the opportunity to request in-network treatment only for the procedure.

If the patient makes that request and out-of-network treatment is still used, the hospital must pay any additional cost to the patient, the patient's group health plan, or the patient's group or individual insurance coverage.

The rule applies as a condition of participating in Medicare, so it would bind essentially every hospital that serves Medicare patients, and it covers any non-emergency examination or treatment scheduled at an in-network hospital.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would have to either guarantee in-network staffing for scheduled procedures or pay the out-of-network charges themselves. That cost pressure could show up as tighter hospital budgets, changes in how hospitals contract with the anesthesiologists, radiologists, and pathologists who work inside them, or higher prices passed back to insurers over time.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals would absorb the cost of out-of-network care they may not directly control, since anesthesiologists and other hospital-based doctors are often independent groups that bill separately; the bill gives hospitals no funding to cover the shift and could push them to restructure those contracts quickly or raise prices elsewhere.

The protection only covers scheduled, non-emergency procedures; emergency care is expressly excluded from the definition, so surprise bills from true emergencies would remain outside this bill's scope.

The bill says nothing about out-of-network facilities or doctors more broadly — it covers procedures at a hospital that is in-network for the patient, so patients treated at out-of-network sites get no protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection for patients is real and targeted: it attacks one of the most cited forms of surprise billing — the unknown out-of-network specialist inside an in-network hospital — and puts the cost on the party, the hospital, that chose the staffing. The honest cost is that hospitals eat a bill they may not currently control, which could mean higher hospital prices or hurried changes to physician staffing contracts. It is a narrow fix, not a broad ban on surprise billing, but the design puts the burden on the party with the leverage to prevent the surprise in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Kennedy introduced the bill on May 22, 2019.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No cosponsors ever joined, and no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and the out-of-network hospital-based physician groups that bill patients directly keep the ability to send surprise balance bills to patients who scheduled care at in-network hospitals. Patients who would have used this protection, and their insurers, gain nothing.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medical Billing Fairness Act and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled committee action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill makes in-network hospitals financially responsible when a patient who requested in-network treatment is treated by an out-of-network provider anyway. Hospitals lose a cost-shifting practice — passing surprise specialist bills to patients — and would have to guarantee in-network staffing or pay the difference themselves.

industries.industry: Hospital-based out-of-network physician groups (anesthesiologists, radiologists, pathologists)
industries.note: These specialists often bill separately from the hospital and generate the surprise bills this bill targets. If the hospital must cover the overage, their leverage to stay out of network and bill patients directly shrinks.
Plans and insurers currently absorb out-of-network overage charges from scheduled procedures; the bill shifts those costs to hospitals.
